---
The first thing my mother bought after she went deaf was a piano. It was an upright, painted a dreadful green, with a cigarette burn on middle C. Three men delivered it on a Wednesday afternoon. By turning it sideways and removing our front door, they got it as far as the bend in the hall, where it stuck. Mother considered this a perfectly good place for a piano. For the next eleven years, anyone coming into our house had to go through the kitchen or be very thin.

She had never played. Before she lost her hearing, her principal interest in music had been getting the people upstairs to turn theirs down. I thought the purchase was an act of defiance, the sort of thing one read about in magazines at the dentist. I told people so. In fact, as she later explained, she had seen it in the window of the hospice shop, and green was her favorite color. I have spent much of my life discovering how often I mistook my mother for a more literary person.

A piano tuner came the following Saturday. He had a little leather bag and a name, Mr. Vale, that suited his profession so well I suspected he had chosen it. He played a scale, opened the top, and took out a teaspoon, two marbles, and an envelope addressed to a woman in Leeds. Then he wrote on his pad: HOW GOOD DO YOU WANT IT?

Mother wrote back: HOW GOOD CAN YOU GET IT FOR FORTY POUNDS?

He took off his coat.

That afternoon was the first time I noticed the hall had a voice of its own. The picture glass buzzed at one pitch; at another, the brass letter flap lifted a little and fell. When Mr. Vale played a low G, the radiator in the upstairs bathroom answered. I was thirteen, and had recently learned in school that everything was made of atoms. This had struck me as unlikely, especially in the case of things like radiators, which were plainly made of radiator. Now I could almost believe it. The whole house seemed loosely assembled and available for comment.

Mother stood with her hand against the side of the piano. When he finished, she paid him forty pounds and gave him the teaspoon. He declined the marbles. The envelope, which was unsealed, contained a recipe for dripping cake and a newspaper clipping about a tortoise that had returned to its owners after six years. Mother posted it. She disliked unfinished business and had complete faith in the ability of the postal service to find a woman in Leeds in possession of a tortoise.

I began playing because there was no other comfortable way to make a telephone call. Our telephone sat on a little shelf above the piano stool, and conversations with my friend Kit tended to involve long pauses while he ate. During these intervals I picked out advertisements and football chants. One evening I managed the first eight notes of the theme from a detective series. Mother, coming in with the washing, stopped, put down the basket, and signed, *Again.*

We were both beginners at signing. For a while our conversations had the quality of telegrams sent during a natural disaster. *Milk gone. Man Thursday. Aunt angry but alive.* Still, *again* was clear enough. I played the eight notes. She set a hand on the piano and tapped the rhythm with her other hand. Then she went upstairs and returned with a fat blue book she had bought for fifty pence along with the instrument. Its title was *The Happy Pianist*. The child on the cover wore a bow tie and had the fixed expression of a boy whose parents were standing just outside the photograph.

My first proper tune was “Lightly Row.” I played it for three weeks. Kit stopped ringing. The people upstairs, in a surprising reversal of our previous relationship, began to knock on the floor. Mother loved it. She liked to stand in the bend of the hall with her shoulder against the wood, eyes shut, while I played the same sixteen bars. I tried playing something else once, to see if she could tell. She opened one eye and signed, *Wrong boat.*

By winter she had discovered that other people liked the piano too. The postman could do a little boogie-woogie. Our neighbor Mrs. Preece knew precisely one Chopin prelude, which she performed at great speed, as if trying to get through a level crossing before the gates came down. A plumber called out to fix the bathroom tap played a hymn so slowly and beautifully that Mother paid his invoice without noticing he had charged us for two visits. It was not a salon. Nobody wore a scarf indoors or discussed Vienna. People came to the kitchen door on some other business and stayed for a cup of tea and a go on the green piano.

Then my cousin Ruth arrived with her cello. She was seventeen, serious, and six feet tall in her stockinged feet. She had been studying a piece by Bach and wanted to know how it sounded outside her bedroom. The answer, at least in our hall, was enormous. The first low note seemed to travel up through the soles of my shoes and rearrange the contents of my pockets. Mother, halfway down the stairs, sat on a step. Ruth played for perhaps four minutes. For once nobody hurried to put the kettle on afterward.

Mother signed something I didn’t know. She had been taking classes on Tuesday evenings and had lately overtaken me.

“What?” I said, forgetting.

She spelled it out on her fingers. *F-L-O-O-R.*

We spent the next hour moving Ruth and her chair about. The effect was strongest on the third stair and weakest by the kitchen door. With her endpin on a particular scuff in the boards, Ruth could make the little bones in Mother’s ankle tickle. Shift the chair six inches and the sensation disappeared. Mother got the chalk and marked the spot. Then she marked the best places to sit. By the time Ruth put her cello away, the hall looked like the scene of a complicated but rather polite murder.

The following Tuesday, Mother brought two friends home from class. The week after, there were five. Some were deaf, some heard perfectly well, and one, a bus driver called Alan, had simply seen a crowd going down our side passage and followed it on the assumption that something was for sale. Ruth played Bach. I played “Lightly Row,” then, under pressure, the detective theme. Alan turned out to have a rich bass voice. He sang “Ol’ Man River” with his palm flat against the upright and forgot most of the words. Nobody minded. The last bus went without him.

An arrangement developed. On the first Tuesday of each month, at seven in the evening, anybody could come and anybody could play, provided they helped with the chairs. We borrowed stacking chairs from the Baptist church and returned them by Thursday, when the Baptists required them for biscuits and an examination of conscience. Kit came back. His father knew somebody with a double bass. Someone else brought a bass drum, an experiment we did not repeat. Mother bought a big roll of lining paper and taped a length to the hall wall. People drew maps of where they felt things: a shiver at the elbow, a flutter under a heel, a buzz in the bridge of the nose. Mrs. Preece drew an excellent nose.

For a while I believed our evenings had solved deafness. This was the kind of conclusion available to a boy who could hear and had solved very little else. I wrote an essay about it at school. My English teacher entered it for a prize offered by the local paper; it won, and a reporter came round to take a photograph of Mother at the piano. He wanted her to look toward the window with an expression of quiet triumph. Mother wanted to know whether he had moved the bins, because it was collection day. The resulting photograph showed a woman apparently gazing toward a brighter future. She was, in reality, watching a refuse lorry reverse over her begonias.

The headline said MUSIC RESTORES A MOTHER’S LOST WORLD. She read it at breakfast with a piece of toast in one hand. I had expected tears. She turned the page and checked the price of a secondhand camping stove.

Later, as I was getting my things for school, she caught my sleeve.

*Nice essay,* she signed. *Whose mother?*

Mine, obviously. I pointed at her.

She shook her head. *Your mother hates that song about the river.*

This was news to me. She went on: *Your mother likes the people. And the green. Write about the green next time.*

At school they gave me a book token and clapped in assembly. I bought a novel about a boy who escaped to sea and did not mention the prize again. For several years afterward I considered the whole affair a lesson about journalism. It took me longer to understand that she had also been telling me something useful about asking a person a question before writing down the answer.

When I left home, the Tuesdays went on without me. I went to university, learned to cook three dishes, fell in love with a woman who considered all three of them soup, and moved into her flat. On my visits home the lining paper gradually filled. A child drew purple feet beside the skirting board. Someone wrote, near the light switch, *Trumpet here, provided Dennis faces the lavatory.* New people appeared in photographs. Alan retired from the buses. Mrs. Preece slowed down, which improved her Chopin considerably. Mother’s signing grew quick and full of jokes I often needed explaining. It was an odd experience to become the least articulate person in the house where I had learned to speak.

One November she slipped outside the chemist’s and broke her hip. She recovered well, according to the surgeon, who did not live in a house with a piano filling its hall. The occupational therapist took one look at the arrangement and said the upright had to go. There was now a walking frame to consider, and whatever its other virtues, a walking frame could not breathe in.

I came home on a Friday to organize matters. Mother had placed an advertisement offering the piano free to anyone who could collect it. There had been fourteen calls, thirteen of them asking if she delivered. The fourteenth was from a woman who wanted it for a pub but wondered if it came in black.

“We could take it apart,” I said.

We were sitting in the kitchen, where she could see my mouth. She signed, *And put it together where?*

This was the difficulty. My flat was on the fourth floor. Ruth lived in Brussels. The Baptist church had two pianos already, one beyond repair and one, according to the minister, beyond forgiveness.

On Saturday morning Mr. Vale came. His leather bag was the same, but he now wore two hearing aids and his eyebrows had become extravagantly long. He removed the front panel and studied the action. He pressed the burned middle C. It gave a serviceable plonk.

“Still got my tuning,” he said.

“Is that good?”

“No. That was eleven years ago.”

He and Mother conferred in writing, as before. I made tea. By the time I came back an agreement had been reached. The soundboard was cracked, the hammers were worn, and the piano had no great future as an instrument. He would take the action for spare parts. A woodworker he knew might find a use for the rest.

I was furious. This took me by surprise. I had spent half my adolescence complaining about having to come in through the kitchen. Yet there I stood, aged twenty-four, prepared to pick a fight with an elderly piano tuner over the integrity of a piece of furniture nobody wanted.

Mother watched my face. *You want it?*

I nodded.

*Where?*

I had no answer.

She went on, *I don’t mind being deaf. I mind being unable to get to my own front door.*

So on Monday the piano came apart. Once the action was out, it looked less like an instrument and more like a cupboard in which someone had unwisely stored a harp. Mr. Vale’s friend took the case. Two men carried the iron frame out to their van. For the first time in eleven years, daylight from the little window above the front door reached the kitchen wall. There was a clean rectangle on the floor surrounded by a dark tide of dirt. We found thirty-seven pence, a bus ticket, and one of the marbles.

That Tuesday was the first Tuesday of the month. I thought people might stay away, but at half past six Alan came through the front door carrying a folding table. Kit followed with a pot of stew. Mrs. Preece brought six little custard tarts, one of which she ate as she was taking off her coat. The chairs arrived from the church. No one had arranged any music. We ate, and afterward Mother dealt cards. By nine she had taken most of Mr. Vale’s small change. The third stair was still a good place to sit, especially if you wanted to see everybody’s hand.

Years later, after Mother died, I helped clear the house. The lining paper came down in brittle strips. I kept the bit with the nose. In the cupboard under the sink I found the blue book, its pages swollen from a leak, the unhappy boy still in his bow tie. I sat on the bare third stair and tried to remember “Lightly Row.” My fingers could do it on my knee, although I could not have sung it for money.

Outside, someone lifted the letter flap and called my name. It was a young woman from three doors down, holding a little green stool. Her grandfather, the woodworker, had made it from the side of the piano. She thought I might want it.

It is in my kitchen now. My daughter stands on it to wash strawberries or inspect whatever is frying. If you turn it over, you can see along one edge a narrow strip of darker green, the paint that never saw daylight. Sometimes people ask why I keep such a battered thing. I used to tell them the long version, with the cello and the chalk marks and the note that made the radiator sing. These days I usually give them my mother’s answer. It’s a good color.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. This is a carefully shaped first-person family story whose recurring objects and scenes build toward a quiet emotional resolution.

## Grounded reading
The voice is wry, observant, and affectionate without making the mother into a symbol of noble adversity. The narrator’s humor—about the piano jammed in the hall, the reporter’s photograph, and the Baptists’ chairs—sits alongside a deeper recognition that he has repeatedly misunderstood her. The story invites the reader to notice how care and belonging can take practical, imperfect forms: a favorite color, a crowded hall, a place to feel the cello’s vibration. Its ending is tender but restrained; the inherited green stool carries the memory without turning it into a grand lesson.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds deafness as a different relation to music and sensation, not a problem neatly solved by music. It dwells on the obstructive green piano, the hall’s vibrations, signing, shared meals, and the people who gather around the instrument. Its moral emphasis is on listening to a person’s own account of what matters: the mother rejects the narrator’s and newspaper’s more dramatic interpretations, saying she likes “the people” and “the green.” The piano’s eventual removal makes room for the mother’s access and agency, while its wood survives in the stool.

## Evidence line
> Mother, coming in with the washing, stopped, put down the basket, and signed, *Again.*

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the distinctive humor, repeated green-piano imagery, and understated correction of the narrator’s assumptions make this a strong, coherent expressive choice in the sample.
